Article 61: Procedure for impeachment of the president

- When a President is to be impeached for violation of the Constitution, the charge shall be preferred by either House of Parliament.

- No such charge shall be preferred unless -

[a] the proposal to prefer such charge is contained in a resolution which has been moved after at least fourteen days' notice in writing signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of the House has been given of their intention to move the resolution, and

[b] such resolution has been passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House.

- When a charge has been so preferred by either House of Parliament, the other House shall investigate the charge or cause the charge to be investigated and the President shall have the right to appear and to be represented at such investigation.

- If as a result of the investigation a resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House by which the charge was investigated or caused to be investigated, declaring that the charge preferred against the President has been sustained, such resolution shall have the effect of removing the President from his office as from the date on which the resolution is so passed.

Article 280 of the Constitution of India provides for a Finance Commission as a quasi-judicial body. It is constituted by the president of India every fifth year or at such an earlier time as he considers necessary.

It is constituted mainly to give its recommendations on distribution of tax revenues between the Union and the States and amongst the States themselves. Two distinctive features of the Commission's work involve redressing the vertical imbalances between the taxation powers and expenditure responsibilities of the centre and the States respectively and equalization of all public services across the States.

The First Finance Commission was constituted vide Presidential Order dated 22.11.1951 under the chairmanship of Shri K.C. Neogy on 6th April, 1952.

As a country develops, it undergoes 'structural change'. In the case of India, the structural change is peculiar. Usually, with development, the share of agriculture declines and the share of industry becomes dominant. At higher levels of development, the service sector contributes more to the GDP than the other two sectors. In India, the share of agriculture in the GDP was more than 50 per cent - as we would expect for a poor country. But by 1990 the share of the service sector was 40.59 per cent, more than that of agriculture or industry, like what we find in developed nations. This phenomenon of growing share of the service sector was accelerated in the post 1991 period.

questions.solution:
The subject of the Passive Voice is changed into the object of the Active Voice. Also, the object of the Passive Voice is changed into the subject of the Active Voice.

The sentence in the Passive voice is in Simple Past tense. So, the sentence in the Active voice should be in Simple Past tense.

There are certain verbs that don't agree with the preposition "by" in Passive form.

They take the preposition which is appropriate to them in Passive voice. In Active voice, the preposition is sometimes removed.

Some of the verbs along with the prepositions (in Passive voice) are given in the table below:
VerbPreposition
Knownto
Surprisedat
Amazedat
Annoyed (somebody)with
Annoyed (something)at
Includedin

For example:

I was annoyed with her. (Passive)

She annoyed me. (Active)

So, options (a) and (d) are eliminated because of the usage of the preposition 'at'.

Option (b) is eliminated because it is in the present tense.

The options except (c) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Active Voice for Simple past tense, i.e., 'Subject + V2 + Object'.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (c): The cross-section of people there surprised me.

The removal of the helping verb ['was' here] and the preposition 'by' is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Passive to Active.

The Passive voice in this question is in Past Indefinite. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Past Indefinite.

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct sentence. A) An effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritised clear and consistent communication. B) A effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritise clear and consistent communication. C) A effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritised clear and consistent communication. D) An effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritise clear and consistent communication.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the grammatically correct sentence.

A) An effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritised clear and consistent communication.

B) A effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritise clear and consistent communication.

C) A effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritised clear and consistent communication.

D) An effective communication strategy builds strong relationships. A successful business must prioritise clear and consistent communication.
questions.solution:
The grammatically correct sentence is D. The error in sentence A is related to the verb form. The modal verb "must" requires the base form of the verb that follows it. But "prioritised" (the past tense form) is incorrect. The correct base form is "prioritise". The error in sentence B is related to article usage. The article "a" should be replaced with the article "an" because "effective" starts with a vowel sound. The article "an" is used before the words that begin with vowel sounds and 'a' is used before the words that begin with consonant sounds. The error in sentence C is related to article usage and verb form. The article "a" should be replaced with "an" because "effective" starts with a vowel sound. Also, the verb "prioritised" is incorrect because "must" requires the base form of the verb. Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Modal verb: A verb used with another verb to express an idea such as possibility that is not expressed by the main verb. The modal verbs in English are "can," "could," "may," "might," "must," "ought," "shall," "should," "will," and "would." They do not change their form (spelling) and they have no infinitive or participle (past/present). Example: I can speak Spanish. Here 'can' expresses the ability of the person to speak (main verb) Spanish. This ability cannot be expressed by the main verb 'speak'.

Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.
